Those high-renewables examples also have special enabling conditions (large hydro resources, favorable geography, or small grids) that don’t generalize to every industrialized region.

Even if renewables can generate a lot of electricity, replacing fossil fuels everywhere runs into system-level constraints: variable generation requires massive grid upgrades, long-duration storage, and demand/backup capacity to cover multi-day and seasonal gaps. The result is that, at least in the near-to-medium term, the grid still needs dispatchable power.

That’s exactly why natural gas—while still a fossil fuel—is an appropriate bridge. Existing gas plants and pipeline/storage infrastructure allow rapid emissions reductions compared with coal and provide the dispatchability that intermittent renewables currently can’t always deliver at large scale. So, a realistic net-zero pathway is sequencing: use gas to cut emissions quickly with today’s infrastructure while scaling renewables and improving the grid, rather than assuming renewables can simply “fill the energy needs” of major countries anytime soon.
